gandhi-ashram-jamalpur.desc: The Gandhi Ashram at Kapasatia in Melandah upazila was founded in the 1930s by local followers of Mahatma Gandhi to promote spinning, weaving, education and self-reliance in villages. It has been restored as a museum, with a small collection of photographs, spinning wheels and documents from the freedom movement. The surrounding grounds are calm and green. It is an unusual stop for travellers interested in South Asian history.
blocks: How to get there
Bus or CNG from Jamalpur town to Melandah, then an auto to Kapasatia.

glance: Bazaars and riverside stalls in Dewanganj and Islampur
jamalpur-char-peanuts.desc: The sandy soil of the Jamuna chars suits peanuts, and they are one of the main dry-season crops in the char villages. After harvest, vendors roast them in pans of hot sand and sell paper cones of warm nuts with salt and chilli. Fresh boiled peanuts are another local snack. It is a simple taste of the river islands.

jamalpur-chhanar-polao.desc: Chhanar polao is a chhana sweet named for its grain-like, pulao-style look, made from local cow's milk and good sugar. Jamalpur's version is known for being noticeably less sweet than most Bangladeshi sweets, which suits people who find rasgolla too sugary. Makers cook it over a wood fire, which they say gives it its particular flavour. Ask for it at the older sweet shops in Jamalpur town.

jamalpur-nakshi-kantha.desc: Nakshi kantha is a quilt made by layering old saris and stitching them together with fine running stitches that form flowers, animals and scenes of village life. Jamalpur has become one of the country's main centres for the craft, with thousands of women working from home for local enterprises. Bed covers, cushion covers, saris and bags are sold in Jamalpur town and in Dhaka. A good piece can take weeks to finish.
blocks: Good to know
Buy from producer groups in Jamalpur town for fair prices to the makers.

jamalpur-burimar-mishti.desc: Burima Mishtanna Bhandar began in Jamalpur town in the late 1940s as a small doi-chira shop opened by Amolabala Saha, whom everyone called Burima. Jute workers were her first regulars, and soon the whole town was buying her sweets; she made them, served customers and kept the accounts herself until she died in 2004. Her grandchildren now run the shop in Amlapara. It makes a dozen or so sweets, including chhoto golla, chomchom, kalojam, para sandesh, date-gur sweets and an unusual green-chilli sweet.

bahadurabad-ghat.desc: Bahadurabad Ghat in Dewanganj upazila was for decades an important rail-ferry crossing over the Jamuna. Though its old role has faded, the riverbank remains a dramatic place, with the Jamuna spreading wide and sandy chars appearing and vanishing with the seasons. Country boats carry people and goods out to the char villages. Sunsets over the braided river are memorable.
blocks: How to get there
Train or bus from Jamalpur town to Dewanganj, then an auto to Bahadurabad.
Good to know
Only take boats in calm weather and with a local boatman.

glance: 170 km to Jamalpur by road, 4–6 hours by bus or car
masjid-e-noor-bakshiganj.desc: Masjid-e-Noor was opened in May 2018 at Daripara, at the edge of Bakshiganj town on the Jamalpur road. A local man, Mahbubul Haque Chishti, paid for it himself, and it was built in the style of Turkish Ottoman mosques, clad in marble, with two storeys and room for about 2,500 worshippers. Its white domes and minarets have made it a popular photo stop for people heading to the Lauchapra hills nearby.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Jamalpur town to Bakshiganj; the mosque is on the right as you enter town on the Jamalpur–Bakshiganj road.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid visiting at prayer times unless you are joining them. Combine it with Lauchapra.

jamalpur-jamuna-chars.desc: The Jamuna on Jamalpur's western side is braided into many channels around low sandy islands called chars. People living here move with the river, rebuilding when floods shift the land. In the dry season they grow peanuts, chilli, maize and pulses on the sand. A boat trip with a local guide shows a side of rural Bangladesh few visitors see.
blocks: How to get there
From Islampur or Dewanganj, hire a boat at a riverside ghat.
Good to know
Go with a local contact, carry water and sun cover, and be respectful when visiting homes.

glance: 170 km to Jamalpur by road, 4–6 hours by bus or car
lauchapra.desc: Lauchapra in Bakshiganj upazila sits at the edge of the Garo Hills, where Jamalpur's flat plains meet low, forested ridges. A recreation area has a viewing tower, picnic spots and small lakes, and the view stretches north to the hills in Meghalaya. Garo and other indigenous families live in nearby villages. It is a favourite winter picnic spot, so weekdays are calmer.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Jamalpur town to Bakshiganj, then a CNG to Lauchapra.
Good to know
Do not wander towards the border; follow local guidance.

glance: 170 km to Jamalpur by road, 4–6 hours by bus or car
dayamoyee-temple-jamalpur.desc: The Dayamoyee temple stands in the centre of Jamalpur town and dates its founding to 1696, which makes it one of the oldest institutions in the town. It is an active place of worship, and during Durga Puja and other festivals the courtyard fills with devotees and visitors. It is an easy stop if you are passing through the district town on the way to Lauchapra or the Jamuna.
blocks: How to get there
In Jamalpur town; any rickshaw from the railway station or bus stand can take you there.
Good to know
Remove shoes before entering the shrine area and dress modestly.

sarishabari-para-sandesh.desc: Para sandesh from Sarishabari is made by boiling milk for hours into thick khir, then cooking it with sugar until it can be shaped into small, firm pieces. It is grainy, rich and less sweet than syrup-soaked sweets. Because it keeps well, people carry it as gifts to Dhaka and beyond. Buy it fresh at Sarishabari's sweet shops.
